review.turning_point: The critical mistake was 9.Be2??, which overlooked the dual attack on f2 and allowed 9...Qxf2+ instead of defending the square with 9.Qd2.
review.focus: Always calculate your opponent's direct mating and checking threats before making quiet developing moves like 9.Be2.

When White blundered with 14.Rg2??, you had the chance to win a pawn and take control. Instead, 14...Nh3? and the trade 15...Qxe1+?? released all the tension. You followed up with 16...Nxf4??, grabbing a pawn but leaving your knight vulnerable, though White let you off the hook with 17.Rf2?? rather than taking the piece immediately.

You got another golden opportunity when White played 23.Nf3??. Instead of cashing in with 23...Nxf3, you played 23...Bg4??, setting up a pin on the f3-knight. White blundered again with 24.Be2??, but you traded with 24...Nxe2?? instead of capturing the pinned knight. sections.text: You opened with Petrov's Defense and navigated the initial symmetrical lines well. After 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Bg5 Be6, you held an equal footing. When White traded on e6, you chose 9...fxe6?!, accepting doubled pawns instead of keeping your structure intact, though you quickly castled queenside with 11...O-O-O to secure your king.

In the middlegame, you pushed pawns on the kingside with 13...h6 and 14...g5?!, trying to gain space. However, White placed their bishop on the dangerous long diagonal with 15.Bg2. After you repositioned your defender with 16...Nd7?!, White zeroed in on your king with 17.Qf3, creating an immediate checkmate battery aimed directly at b7.

You needed to defend the b7-square immediately with 17...c6 to blunt the bishop's diagonal. Instead, you pushed 17...h5??, missing White's direct threat entirely. White ended the game instantly on the next turn with 18.Qxb7#.

review.focus: Always check your opponent's direct threats against your king before continuing your own pawn pushes, especially after moves like 17.Qf3 that align queen and bishop on your castled position.

But when Black hit your bishop with 5...Ne5, you pushed 6.f4?? without guarding your piece, allowing 6...Nxc4 and dropping a full bishop right out of the opening.

Down material, you tried to generate threats with 8.Qh5?! creating a pin on the f7-pawn and the e8-king. Black defended calmly, but after 10.Nf5, they gave you a lifeline with 10...O-O?. Rather than taking advantage, you traded on e7 with 11.Nxe7+?! and then retreated with 12.Nf5?!, leaving your pieces exposed.

Black immediately took over the open e-file with 12...Re8. After 13.Qd4?! pinning the d7-pawn, Black struck with 13...Rxe4+. You played the forced recapture 14.Qxe4! Nxe4, which left you down a queen. After 17.Nc3?! Bxf5, another piece was won by Black, and the game was out of reach.

review.turning_point: The decisive moment arrived on 6.f4??, where neglecting the direct attack on your bishop cost a piece and forced you onto the defensive.
review.focus: Always respond to immediate threats before advancing pawns; on 6.f4??, retreating the attacked bishop with 6.Be2 would have preserved your opening advantage.

sections.text: You opened well against the Vienna, developing smoothly and putting early pressure on White's knights. With 7...Bxc3+, you targeted a piece on c3 that was pinned against the a1-rook, but trading it off prematurely resolved White's tension without gaining much in return. Under pressure, you tried to relieve tension by trading off on f3, but capturing the bishop with 15...gxf5 ripped open the defenses around your king completely. White jumped on the opportunity immediately with 16.Qh5, creating unavoidable mating threats starting with 17.Qxh7+.

review.turning_point: The game tipped decisively with 10...Nxg4, giving up a piece for pawns and opening attacking lines that White quickly used against your king.
review.focus: Avoid sacrificing material speculatively when your opponent's king isn't in immediate danger, as seen on 10...Nxg4.

review.headline: A sharp gambit gone wrong in the opening

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4, and Black challenged your center right away with 1...d5. Against the Scandinavian Defense, the standard and most reliable approach is simply 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3, gaining a tempo on the queen while developing a piece. Instead, you chose 2.Nf3, heading into the Tennison Gambit.

After Black took the pawn with 2...dxe4, the critical idea of the gambit is to immediately relocate the attacked knight with 3.Ng5 to target the e4 pawn. Instead, you played 3.d3, leaving your knight on f3 entirely unprotected. Black accepted the free piece with 3...exf3.

Down a full knight, you developed your bishop with 4.Be3, but Black grabbed another pawn with 4...fxg2, leaving you down a piece and multiple pawns with your kingside compromised. You decided to resign after move 4.

review.turning_point: The decisive mistake was 3.d3, which overlooked the basic capture of your knight on f3 instead of saving the piece with 3.Ng5.
review.focus: When playing aggressive gambits like 2.Nf3, always ensure you know the intended retreat squares for your attacked pieces so you don't drop material on move 3.

review.headline: A sharp Sicilian opening slips away after a loose knight tactic

sections.text: You stepped straight into an Open Sicilian and quickly claimed central space. When Black brought their queen out early with 5...Qxc5, you gained rapid piece development. You pushed in the center with 14.e5, and Black's retreat 14...Nd7 handed you a clear advantage. You punished it cleanly with 15.exd6, winning the pawn back and leaving Black's king side under severe pressure.

With active pieces, you looked for an aggressive breakthrough. However, 18.Nd6 allowed 18...Qc7, walking right into a tactical trap. Instead of retreating or defending, you played 19.Nxb7, creating a discovered attack from the queen on c7 against your bishop on f4. After 19...Qxf4, your knight was stranded on b7 and Black took the initiative.

You attempted to salvage the stranded knight by offering a queen trade with 20.Qe3, which created a pin against the e6-pawn, but Black simply replied 20...Qc7 to trap your knight. You fought back resourcefully with 21.Bxe6, utilizing the pin on the f7-pawn to grab material back. However, after 21...Qxb7 22.Bxd7 Qxd7, you were down a piece, and Black maintained control until your clock ran out.

review.turning_point: The game swung on 19.Nxb7, which left your bishop on f4 hanging to 19...Qxf4 and ultimately lost your knight on the rim.
review.focus: Before playing an uncoordinated tactical capture like 19.Nxb7, always check if your supporting pieces are left unprotected.

Fortunately, White gifted you the initiative with 10.dxc5, and you jumped on it with 10...Naxc5!, instantly activating your knight and freeing your position.

You coordinated your pieces cleanly with ...b6, ...Bb7, and ...Rac8. After 17.Qg3, 17...g6 was an unnecessary concession when trading queens with 17...Qxg3 was much stronger. However, you stayed alert, and when White misplayed with 19.Qh3, you struck with the central fork 19...Qxe4, hitting both minor pieces and winning the e2-bishop two moves later.

Ahead in material, you ruthlessly dismantled White's defenses. You scooped up pawns on b2 and c2, piling on overwhelming pressure. White tried a desperate sacrifice with 25.Qxe6, but you stayed cool, eliminating defenders and forcing checkmate on g2.

review.turning_point: White's blunder 19.Qh3 handed you complete control, allowing 19...Qxe4 to fork White's pieces and collapse their position.
review.focus: Look for active central strikes in the opening rather than passive retreat moves like 4...Nfd7.
